name: Scaling from 6 lakes to all Bengaluru lakes

identity.method_name: City-scale extension of the current 6-lake / 42-row Sentinel-2 pipeline to all Bengaluru lakes, paired with the 2024-2026 Karnataka government lake-encroachment survey as an external ground-truth label source
identity.core_idea: Replace the current 6-lake OpenStreetMap fence with a city-wide set of lake polygons (roughly 183-211 lakes depending on jurisdiction, see below), rerun the SAME MNDWI/NDVI/OSM-intrusion pipeline for all of them across the same 2019-2025 window, and -- the pivotal upgrade this item actually investigates -- attach a REAL external label per lake drawn from the Karnataka Minor Irrigation Department / State Survey Settlement and Land Records (SSLR) Department's 2024-2026 Supreme-Court-directed encroachment survey. If that survey's per-lake output can genuinely be obtained, this converts the project from a purely unsupervised, unlabelled 42-row exercise into a supervised problem with a real government-sourced label at roughly n=183-211 lakes -- not simply a bigger unlabelled table.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None exists in machine-readable, citable form for the core object of this item (a per-lake Bengaluru encroachment label set). Related, non-dataset-ID references found: BBMP Lakes Monitoring System, a web application at lms.bbmpgov.in with per-lake report pages but no confirmed public dataset export (this research could not reach the portal directly -- TLS certificate error -- so this is carried over from, and consistent with, the sibling item B2's finding). OpenStreetMap water-body extraction has no formal dataset ID; it is obtained ad hoc via the Overpass API querying natural=water / water=lake / landuse=reservoir tags clipped to a Bengaluru administrative boundary. The Sentinel-2 imagery pipeline itself is unchanged from the project's existing setup (COPERNICUS/S2_SR_HARMONIZED via Earth Search STAC / AWS, tile MGRS-43PGQ, per project_constraints).

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: This item is a direct attempt to answer the project's single organising question. If the Minor Irrigation/SSLR survey's per-lake output can be obtained (status: unconfirmed, see part (c) below), the strategy shifts from the project's current 'threshold rule' / 'fully unsupervised' footing to genuine transfer from an external labelled administrative dataset -- the single most valuable methodological upgrade identified anywhere in this research programme, because it is the only route in the entire outline that could give the project real ground truth rather than another proxy. Cost: it is currently unconfirmed whether a machine-readable or even tabular per-lake output of that survey exists publicly; if it does not, the fallback is manually transcribing figures lake-by-lake from news coverage and any obtainable government documents, realistically a multi-week task for the ~183-211 BBMP-jurisdiction lakes, not a data-download task.
fit_to_project.input_required: (1) A complete, deduplicated list of lake identities across the chosen jurisdiction -- this does not exist as a single number (see part (a): credible figures found range from 183 to 837 to over 41,000 depending on jurisdiction and year). (2) A boundary polygon per lake at usable spatial accuracy -- obtainable in part from OpenStreetMap extraction, but OSM's coverage of Bengaluru's smaller/informal tanks is known, from this project's own experience with its 6 lakes, to be incomplete, so the remainder would need manual digitising from basemap imagery. (3) The Minor Irrigation/SSLR survey's actual per-lake output -- existence confirmed by 2025-2026 news reporting, public machine-readable availability NOT confirmed (see part (c)). (4) The same Sentinel-2 imagery the project already fetches -- already available, and, per part (d) below, at near-zero marginal cost since the whole city fits inside the tile(s) the project already indexes.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: not applicable in the intended sense -- this item exists specifically to replace the 42-row dataset, not to operate within it. If pursued, the new effective sample size is roughly 183-211 lakes (BBMP-jurisdiction scope) if evaluated at the lake level, or up to about 1,300-1,477 lake-year rows if kept as a 7-year panel -- but see part (e): because the survey label is very likely a single cross-sectional snapshot, the number of INDEPENDENTLY LABELLED units remains the lake count (~183-211), not the lake-year count, so 'more rows' does not by itself mean 'more independent labelled examples'.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: needs-weak-labels currently, pending confirmation of part (c). If the survey link fails, the scaled-up boundary set is still useful as a much larger sample for the SAME unsupervised/proxy methods already used at n=42 (more statistical power for detecting population-level patterns, e.g. trend tests across lakes), but it does NOT by itself solve the project's stated 'no ground truth' limitation -- only a successful part (c) outcome would do that.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Yes for the imagery side -- the Sentinel-2/20 m pipeline is unchanged and scales without a resolution problem. No resolution issue exists on the label side either, since the survey/label data is an administrative/legal record (acres, occupancy status), not a raster -- but it does require a genuine UNIT reconciliation, not a resolution fix: the survey reports areas in acres against cadastral/revenue boundaries, while the project's own pipeline reports areas in hectares against OpenStreetMap or manually digitised polygons, and these two boundary definitions will not agree exactly lake by lake.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: Karnataka Minor Irrigation Department / State Survey Settlement and Land Records (SSLR) Department 2024-2026 digital lake survey (Supreme-Court-directed; per Times of India, 11 Jan 2026, led by SSLR Commissioner J Manjunath, launched March 2024, roughly 95% complete for Bengaluru Urban district as of the article date) -- IF its per-lake tabular output can be obtained. No confirmed public download of that output was located in this research; it is described in news coverage as being uploaded to an internal 'Web GIS platform', whose public accessibility is unconfirmed. Absent that, 'none confirmed'.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Directly targets limitation (1) 'only 42 rows' -- the project's own named main blocker -- by design. Has a real but conditional secondary effect on limitation (3) 'no real ground truth', entirely contingent on part (c) succeeding. Does not address limitation (2) (OpenStreetMap buildings are still a single 2026 snapshot even at city scale) or limitation (4) (still one dry-season Sentinel-2 scene per year, unchanged by adding more lakes).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: Not directly, but with a genuine benefit worth naming: if the survey distinguishes GOVERNMENT-AGENCY encroachment (which the New Indian Express reporting shows it does -- 288 of 472 acres attributed to government agencies including BBMP/BDA/BWSSB/Namma Metro) from PRIVATE encroachment (184-188 acres in the same report), that split is a genuinely useful cross-check against the sibling item D7's desilting confound, since a lake flagged as 'government-agency occupied' may reflect legitimate public-works activity (potentially including desilting yards or maintenance access) rather than illegal private construction -- worth checking per lake, but this is a partial cross-check, not a full resolution of D7's problem.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No -- unrelated to the vegetation-versus-open-water spectral separation problem.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: This is the central positive finding of this whole item. IF the Minor Irrigation/SSLR survey's per-lake output can be obtained, it would be categorically the most legally traceable data source identified anywhere in this research programme: it is a government survey conducted under direct Supreme Court supervision (directions dated 21 July 2023 and 1 August 2023, per New Indian Express), with named departmental leadership and an explicit GPS/drone/ArcGIS/rover-based methodology -- stronger provenance than OpenStreetMap, stronger than any remote-sensing proxy, and arguably stronger than the KTCDA/Bhuvan/National Wetland Atlas sources examined in the sibling item B2, none of which was confirmed there to have a public download. This is precisely why part (c) is flagged as the single highest-value question in this entire research programme: it is the one plausible path to genuine legal ground truth, not just a better boundary.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: The survey is fundamentally a SINGLE cross-sectional exercise: launched March 2024, about 95% complete as of January 2026, with no evidence found in this research of a recurring annual re-survey cycle at the same rigor. So even in the best case where part (c) succeeds, the result is ONE label per lake as of roughly 2024-2026, not seven annual labels matching the project's 2019-2025 study years -- this materially changes the honest structure of any resulting dataset (see part (e) and the evaluation section below).

implementation.libraries: geopandas, osmnx or overpy (OpenStreetMap/Overpass extraction), pandas plus rapidfuzz/fuzzywuzzy (reconciling lake names across OSM, BBMP LMS and the survey, which will not share a common ID), the project's existing Sentinel-2/rasterio/xarray pipeline unchanged, QGIS for manual boundary digitising and QA of the polygons OSM is missing or draws badly.
implementation.licence: OpenStreetMap data: ODbL, attribution and share-alike required, no problem for academic use. Sentinel-2 imagery: unchanged, open Copernicus terms. The Minor Irrigation/SSLR survey data's licence/redistribution terms are entirely unknown and [uncertain] pending ever seeing an actual data file -- if obtained via a written request or RTI application, treat it as a public record citable for academic purposes, but do not assume open redistribution rights without confirming them from whoever supplies it.
implementation.compute_requirement: CPU-only and modest for the imagery side. The current pipeline already processes a scene subset for a 22x17 km (374 km2) box (~900,000 pixels/scene per project_constraints); the whole former-BBMP city extent (roughly 700-800 km2) up to the larger Bengaluru Urban district (roughly 2,190 km2) both sit comfortably inside the single MGRS-43PGQ Sentinel-2 tile (110 km x 110 km, 12,100 km2) the project already indexes, or at most one adjoining tile -- meaning the SAME already-relevant Sentinel-2 scenes cover essentially all ~183-837 candidate lakes regardless of which jurisdiction is chosen, so NO new satellite passes need to be fetched, only a larger crop/AOI and many more polygons to run zonal statistics against. Reprocessing a full-tile-sized raster (roughly 30 million 20 m pixels versus the current ~900,000) with simple band math (MNDWI, NDVI) is still trivial on a laptop CPU, well under an hour per scene, no GPU required, comfortably inside free Colab/Kaggle/Earth Engine quotas. The real bottleneck, confirmed by this analysis, is NOT compute -- it is boundary curation and label linkage, below.
implementation.student_days: Pipeline re-run/re-parameterisation to a larger AOI and more polygons: 1-3 days, mostly debugging edge cases (lakes split across tile boundaries, very small or irregular tanks). Boundary curation is the dominant, and likely prohibitive-in-full, cost: a conservative estimate is 0.25-0.5 student-day per lake for the subset with adequate existing OSM geometry, rising to roughly 1 day per lake for the many smaller/informal tanks needing manual digitising from basemap imagery -- across ~183-211 BBMP-jurisdiction lakes this totals roughly 40-100 student-days if done rigorously by one student, i.e. WEEKS, not days, and is probably impractical to do in full within a solo B.Tech timeline. Label linkage (matching survey records to boundaries by name/ward, resolving inconsistent lake naming across sources) adds a further 5-15 student-days, but only IF a usable tabular survey output is ever obtained -- if it is not, this cost disappears but so does the item's entire labelling benefit. A realistic compromise is a PARTIAL scale-up of roughly 20-40 additional lakes rather than the full ~200, cutting boundary-curation cost to roughly 10-20 student-days while still multiplying the current sample by 3-7x.

evaluation.metrics: IF a real per-lake label is obtained: for a binary 'documented encroachment: yes/no' label, precision/recall/F1/AUROC of the remote-sensing pipeline's own encroachment flag against that label; for a continuous 'encroached acres' label, RMSE/MAE/Spearman correlation between the pipeline's footprint-loss estimate and the survey's own encroached-acreage figure. WITHOUT the label (the likely partial outcome), only the project's existing internal/proxy metrics remain, now computed over a larger N, which increases statistical power for population-level claims but still cannot validate accuracy against a real target.
evaluation.validation_protocol: Because the survey label is a single cross-sectional snapshot (see temporal_granularity), the honest primary evaluation unit is LAKE-LEVEL (N is approximately 183-211), using k-fold or leave-one-out cross-validation grouped BY LAKE, since there is only one label per lake. If the pipeline is instead run as a lake-year panel with that single label broadcast identically across all 7 years for a given lake, any split that is not grouped by lake (leave-one-lake-out) will leak the constant label across a lake's own train and test rows and inflate reported performance -- this is exactly the same lake-clustering leakage problem the project's own dataset already has at n=42 (see the sibling item C3 on mixed-effects models), reproduced at a larger scale, not eliminated by scaling up.
evaluation.leakage_risk: (1) Label-broadcast leakage described above -- a lake's single static label repeated across its 7 rows. (2) Spatial autocorrelation between neighbouring lakes sharing the same rajakaluve/catchment network, since an upstream lake's encroachment or desilting status can mechanically affect a downstream lake's water level, so even lake-level (grouped) splits are not fully statistically independent. (3) Name-matching leakage during manual reconciliation of ambiguous lake names between OSM and the survey -- if the student resolves an ambiguous match while already aware of which lakes the survey flagged as heavily encroached, that human-in-the-loop step can inject label information into how a boundary is drawn (e.g. unconsciously drawing a smaller 'current' boundary for a lake already known to have shrunk); this linkage step should be done blind to the survey's encroachment figures wherever practical.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: With a genuine external label successfully obtained, conformal prediction (the project's own item C7) becomes directly and meaningfully applicable for the first time in this research programme, since a real calibration target would finally exist; report coverage against a held-out set of lakes. Without the label, uncertainty reporting is unchanged from the current 42-row situation -- there remains no target to calibrate against.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not directly applicable, but flag one specific temptation this scale-up creates: once ~200 lakes give more rows, there may be a temptation to synthetically back-fill a yearly label for 2019-2025 from the single 2024-2026 survey snapshot (e.g. by assuming linear encroachment growth). This would fabricate a plausible but entirely invented temporal label and must never be presented as if it were the survey's own ground truth; if ever attempted, it must be explicitly disclosed as a modelling assumption, not as data.

evidence.published_performance: Not a model-performance item; the relevant 'evidence' here is the set of competing lake-count and encroachment figures found, each tiered by source credibility. (a) REAL AUTHORITATIVE COUNT: no single authoritative current figure exists. Verified-to-news-report-level figures found in this research, from a 2020 government-linked report cited by Wikipedia: 211 lakes within BBMP boundary limits [verify, secondary/tertiary sourcing via Wikipedia, primary report not directly located]; a 2015 survey of Bangalore Urban district: 834 lakes [verify]; a 2018 count by an unnamed autonomous Karnataka government institute: 1,521 water bodies in the Bangalore Metropolitan Area, of which 837 were disused [verify]; historical counts of 127 lakes (1986 Lakshman Rau Committee, 90 transferred to the Forest Department), 2,789 lakes (2001, BMRDA limits, 2-50 ha size class), 3,578 tanks/lakes (2013, Minor Irrigation Department, apparently a wider count), 596 (2013, BDA), and 1,545 lakes (2014-16, Koliwad Committee) [all verify, secondary/tertiary sourcing]. Credible current Indian news reporting, tiered explicitly by source strength: TIER 1 (named government department and official, court-linked) -- Times of India, 11 Jan 2026: 837 total water bodies in Bengaluru URBAN DISTRICT (not BBMP city limits), surveyed by the Minor Irrigation Department and State Survey Settlement and Land Records (SSLR) Department under SSLR Commissioner J Manjunath, a digital survey launched March 2024 and about 95% complete, using drones, satellite imagery, ArcGIS mapping and rover-based ground verification, with 730 of 837 (about 90%) found under illegal occupation and 4,229 acres affected; statewide figures in the same report: 14,442 of 41,849 water bodies encroached, 43,307 acres affected. TIER 1 (named official, Supreme-Court-linked, but city-limits scope) -- New Indian Express, 29 July 2025: 183 total lakes under BBMP jurisdiction, citing Supreme Court directions dated 21 July 2023 and 1 August 2023, survey conducted by Revenue Department Assistant Director of Land Records (ADLR) staff, 136 of 183 lakes surveyed as of the article date (33 pending), finding 472 acres encroached (288 acres by government agencies including BBMP/BDA/BWSSB/Namma Metro, 184-188 acres by private persons [figure varies slightly across the source extract retrieved]), with 17.38 acres reclaimed and encroachments removed on 29 water bodies. TIER 2 (credible news outlet, no named survey/agency given in the article itself) -- Bangalore Mirror (retrieved via this research as roughly 8 months old relative to a September 2026 vantage, i.e. approximately January 2026): 202 lakes total in the city, of which 183 are functional and 19 have disappeared entirely; 851.11 acres remain encroached, 949.26 acres affected overall, only 38.09 acres cleared, and 172 lakes have had their mandated 30 m buffer zone reduced under the Karnataka Lake Conservation and Development Authority Act, 2024 [uncertain whether this is a renamed KTCDA or a distinct body; not independently confirmed in this session]. TIER 2 (credible news outlet, same underlying 837-lake population as the Tier-1 TOI figure but a stricter severity threshold) -- a separate Bangalore Mirror piece (retrieved as roughly 5 months old relative to September 2026, i.e. approximately April 2026): '12% of Bengaluru's 837 lakes face existential crisis due to encroachment', suggesting the underlying dataset records SEVERITY tiers (any illegal occupation, about 90%, versus 'existential crisis' severity, about 12%), and that different articles reporting different tiers of the same survey are not necessarily contradictory once this is understood. (c) THE '159 OF 202' CLAIM NAMED IN THE TASK NOTE: this research could NOT verify it. Multiple targeted searches for '159 of 202', '159 lakes', and combinations with 'encroachment', 'BBMP' and '202' returned no matching government page, primary source, or news article of any tier. The verified figures above are numerically DIFFERENT from '159 of 202' in every case (136 of 183; 202 lakes total with acreage, not a lake-count-encroached figure; 730 of 837; 90% of 837 or 12% of 837). It is plausible the task's '159 of 202' figure is an interim milestone of the SAME ongoing Revenue/SSLR survey reported at a rollout stage this research's search paths did not index (the NIE piece shows 136/183 in July 2025 and TOI shows 95% of 837 by January 2026, so a '159 of 202' checkpoint could plausibly sit somewhere on that timeline), or a conflation/rounding by a secondary summary not traced here, or drawn from a specific document (a BBMP press release, a Karnataka Legislative Assembly reply, or a court filing) outside what this session's search tooling could reach. This figure should be treated as UNVERIFIED and not used as a citable statistic; the tiered, sourced figures above should be used instead, each correctly attributed to its own jurisdiction, date and survey round.
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: All figures found are Bengaluru-specific by construction, at three genuinely DIFFERENT jurisdictional scales that must not be conflated: former-BBMP city limits (approximately 183-211 lakes across sources), the wider Bengaluru Urban district (approximately 834-837 lakes), and statewide Karnataka (approximately 41,849 water bodies). The remaining risk this item must guard against is exactly this within-Bengaluru jurisdictional scale-mismatch -- a BBMP-limits figure (e.g. 183 lakes, 472 acres encroached) must never be presented as if it described the much larger Bengaluru Urban district population (837 lakes, 4,229 acres), since they are different survey populations conducted by different combinations of departments.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: Yes, by construction -- this item's entire subject is Bengaluru itself, so it is not a transplanted method needing an applicability check in the way other items in this research programme require. Comparable government-run, court-directed lake/tank encroachment surveys in other Indian cities (e.g. Hyderabad's Full Tank Level encroachment litigation, Chennai's Pallikaranai/Chembarambakkam lake-boundary disputes) were not investigated in this research and may offer useful methodological precedent for how such surveys eventually get published or litigated, but this is [uncertain / out of scope] for this item.
evidence.evidence_recency: Very recent and, on the current-relevant claims, well within range: the strongest evidence (Times of India, 11 January 2026; Bangalore Mirror pieces from roughly January and April 2026; New Indian Express, 29 July 2025) is all from 2025-2026, describing an ongoing 2024-2026 government survey. Historical lake-count figures (1986, 2001, 2013, 2014-16, 2018, 2020) are used only for HISTORICAL CONTEXT on how the count has been measured differently over time, not as the load-bearing current evidence, so no pre-2020 reliance flag applies to the item's core finding.
evidence.primary_sources: New Indian Express, 29 Jul 2025, '472 acres of lake land encroached in Bengaluru, but only 17 acres reclaimed': https://www.newindianexpress.com/cities/bengaluru/2025/Jul/29/472-acres-of-lake-land-encroached-in-bengaluru-but-only-17-acres-reclaimed (tier: credible Indian news, quoting a named BBMP official and citing specific Supreme Court directions -- direct fetch of the original domain failed in this session; content retrieved via a text-extraction proxy and not independently cross-checked against a second copy, [verify]). Times of India, 11 Jan 2026, 'Encroachments gobble up 730 of 837 lakes in Bengaluru Urban: Survey': https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/bengaluru/encroachments-gobble-up-730-of-837-lakes-in-bengaluru-urban-survey/articleshow/126456722.cms (same caveat: retrieved via a text-extraction proxy, not the original domain, [verify]). Bangalore Mirror, 'Curious case of vanishing lakes': https://bangaloremirror.indiatimes.com/bangalore/cover-story/curious-case-of-vanishing-lakes/heroesshow/126625024.cms (same caveat, [verify], and this article names no survey/agency source for its own figures). Bangalore Mirror, '12% of Bengaluru's 837 lakes face existential crisis due to encroachment': https://bangaloremirror.indiatimes.com/bangalore/others/12-of-bengalurus-837-lakes-face-existential-crisis-due-to-encroachment/articleshow/129909198.cms (found via search snippet only, full content not retrieved in this session, [uncertain]). Wikipedia, 'Lakes of Bangalore' (aggregation of historical committee/survey lake-count figures cited above, each traceable in principle to an underlying government committee report that was not independently located or verified in this session): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakes_of_Bangalore [verify each historical figure against its primary committee report]. BBMP Lakes Monitoring System: https://lms.bbmpgov.in/lake (not reachable in this session, TLS certificate error, [uncertain] on current content/data-export capability, consistent with the sibling item B2's finding).

risk.failure_modes: (1) Committing to the full ~183-211 lake (or larger, ~837) boundary rebuild before confirming the label question in part (c) -- this would spend most of the student's remaining time on boundary curation for a dataset that, if the label never materialises, only helps the SAME unsupervised methods already in use at n=42, at a much higher labour cost. (2) Citing the '159 of 202' figure, or any other specific figure found here, without disclosing its verification tier -- a panel or reviewer catching an uncited or unverifiable number in the write-up is a serious credibility risk. (3) Broadcasting the single 2024-2026 survey label identically across all 7 study years and presenting the resulting ~1,300-1,477 rows as independently labelled -- this is pseudoreplication and will not survive scrutiny. (4) Conflating BBMP-jurisdiction lake counts (approximately 183-211) with Bengaluru Urban district counts (approximately 834-837) when stating 'the number of Bengaluru lakes' -- these are genuinely different populations surveyed by different combinations of departments and must be kept separate in any write-up.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask two hard questions in sequence. First: 'how many lakes are there, really?' -- answerable honestly only by naming the jurisdiction and year for whichever figure is quoted, since this research confirms no single number is authoritative. Second, and more consequential: 'if you now have 200 lakes, do you have 200 real labels, or did you just multiply your unlabelled row count?' -- the honest, defensible answer depends entirely on whether the Minor Irrigation/SSLR survey's Web GIS output can actually be obtained, which this research could NOT confirm. The project must be prepared to report either a genuine success (a labelled n approximately 183-211 lake dataset with a named, court-linked government source) or an honest partial result (a larger but still unlabelled boundary set, useful only for the same proxy methods already used at n=42).
risk.honest_expectation: The realistic, honestly reportable outcome within a solo B.Tech timeline is a PARTIAL scale-up -- roughly 20-40 additional lakes with usable OSM or manually digitised boundaries, chosen to include a spread of sizes and, where possible, lakes with a documented encroachment status from the news reporting gathered here -- rather than the full approximately 183-211, because full-scale boundary curation alone costs tens of student-days that would consume most of the remaining project time. In parallel, sending a single written request or Right to Information Act, 2005 application to the Karnataka Minor Irrigation Department / SSLR Department for the digital lake-survey's per-lake output is a low-cost, high-value action item that should be sent early, regardless of whether the full scale-up is attempted, since its success or failure directly determines whether this project can ever obtain real ground truth. A null result on the label question -- 'we requested the data and either did not receive it in time, or received only aggregate rather than per-lake figures' -- is a valid, reportable, and honestly-disclosed finding, and would still leave the larger boundary set as a legitimate, if unlabelled, contribution.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time for the full pipeline rebuild, gated on the outcome of one specific ADOPT-rated sub-action rated separately and urgently: send the Minor Irrigation Department / SSLR Department request or RTI application for per-lake survey data NOW, in parallel with all other project work, because it is the single highest-value, lowest-cost action identified anywhere in this research programme. If that request succeeds in time, prioritise the pipeline scale-up as the project's headline contribution; if it does not, fall back to the partial 20-40 lake scale-up as a still-worthwhile, lower-risk improvement over the current 6-lake, 42-row dataset.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: There is no single authoritative count of Bengaluru's lakes (roughly 183-211 under the former BBMP limits versus roughly 834-837 across the wider Bengaluru Urban district, depending on source and year), the specific '159 of 202 encroached' figure could not be verified against any primary or news source found in this research, but a real Supreme-Court-directed government survey (Minor Irrigation Department / State Survey Settlement and Land Records Department, 2024-2026, about 95% complete) does exist with per-lake GPS boundaries and encroachment data reportedly uploaded to an internal Web GIS platform -- obtaining that platform's per-lake output, via direct request or RTI application, is the single highest-value next step in this entire project, worth pursuing before committing the tens of student-days a full city-wide boundary rebuild would otherwise cost.
